q: How does the 1.1 deck define Artificial Intelligence?
choices: The field of building systems that perform tasks normally requiring human intelligence
The field of building systems that learn only from labelled input–output examples
The field of building multi-layer neural networks that learn abstract features
The field of building faster hardware to run hand-written human programs
why: AI is the broad goal: systems that perceive, reason, learn and act, by any means. Learning from labels is supervised ML, and multi-layer networks are deep learning; both are only subsets.

q: Which is NOT one of the four AI capabilities listed in 1.1?
choices: Compile
Perceive
Reason
Act

q: A spam filter that gets sharper over time is the deck's example of which capability?
choices: Learn
Perceive
Reason
Act
why: Learn means improving performance from experience. The deck's other examples: Perceive is recognising a face, Reason is diagnosing a fault, Act is a self-driving car steering and braking.

q: What happened in 1956 on the deck's AI timeline?
choices: The Dartmouth Workshop coined the term 'Artificial Intelligence'
Turing proposed the 'Imitation Game' as a test of machine intelligence
Deep Blue defeated the world chess champion Garry Kasparov
The first 'AI winter' began as funding and hype collapsed
why: 1956 is the Dartmouth Workshop. The Imitation Game was 1950, Deep Blue was 1997, and the two AI winters were in the 1970s–80s.

q: In which year did Turing propose the 'Imitation Game'?
why: 1950 is Turing. 1956 is the Dartmouth Workshop, 1959 is Arthur Samuel's ML definition (1.2), and 1997 is Deep Blue.

choices: AlexNet
AlphaGo
Deep Blue
ChatGPT

q: What were the two 'AI winters' of the 1970s–80s?
choices: Periods when AI funding and hype collapsed
Periods when governments banned AI research
Periods when neural networks beat humans at games
Periods when AI hardware was replaced by GPUs
why: The timeline describes them as funding and hype collapsing. GPUs and game-playing wins come much later (2012, 2016).

q: Which nesting of AI, machine learning and deep learning is correct?
choices: DL ⊂ ML ⊂ AI
ML ⊂ DL ⊂ AI
AI ⊂ ML ⊂ DL
DL ⊂ AI ⊂ ML
why: AI is the broadest goal, ML is a subset of AI, and DL is a subset of ML that uses multi-layer neural networks.

q: A chess program built only from hand-coded expert rules, with no learning from data, is…
choices: AI, but not machine learning
Machine learning, but not AI
Deep learning, since it plays games
Neither AI nor machine learning
why: AI covers intelligent behaviour 'however that's achieved, including hand-coded rules'. ML specifically learns patterns from data instead of following hand-written rules, so this is AI but not ML.

q: What distinguishes deep learning within machine learning?
choices: Multi-layer neural networks learning increasingly abstract representations
Hand-written expert rules organised into a very deep decision tree
Agents learning from rewards and penalties in an environment
Algorithms grouping unlabelled data by similarity into clusters
why: The deck defines DL as a subset of ML that uses multi-layer neural networks to learn increasingly abstract representations. The other options describe rule-based AI, RL and clustering.

q: Which is NOT one of the six disciplines said to compose most of AI?
choices: Database administration
Knowledge representation
Automated reasoning
Robotics
why: The six are NLP, knowledge representation, automated reasoning, machine learning, computer vision and speech recognition, and robotics.

q: What is the order of the deck's five-stage machine learning pipeline?
choices: Collect → Train → Evaluate → Deploy & predict → Monitor & retrain
Collect → Evaluate → Train → Monitor & retrain → Deploy & predict
Train → Collect → Deploy & predict → Evaluate → Monitor & retrain
Collect → Train → Deploy & predict → Evaluate → Monitor & retrain
why: You evaluate on unseen data before deploying, then monitor and retrain. The deck stresses that this is a loop: production models are retrained as new data arrives.

q: Supervised learning learns from…
choices: Labelled examples: each input paired with its correct answer
Unlabelled data, which it groups or compresses by similarity
Rewards and penalties received from acting in an environment
Hand-written rules supplied directly by a domain expert
why: Supervised learning sees many (input, correct output) pairs and learns the mapping. The second option is unsupervised learning and the third is reinforcement learning.

q: Flagging unusual patterns in network traffic or transactions is the deck's example of which paradigm?
choices: Unsupervised learning
Supervised learning
Reinforcement learning
Generative AI
why: Anomaly detection is listed under unsupervised learning, next to customer segmentation and topic discovery. There are no labels: the model finds structure on its own.

q: Which loop describes reinforcement learning?
choices: Observe state → act and receive a reward → update strategy to maximise reward
Feed unlabelled data → group it by similarity → patterns emerge on their own
Show (input, output) pairs → learn the mapping → predict labels for new inputs
Tokenize text → predict the next token → generate output one token at a time
why: RL is an agent acting in an environment and learning from rewards and penalties (e.g. AlphaGo, robots learning to walk, data-centre cooling). The others are unsupervised, supervised and LLM pipelines.

q: Deep learning has existed in theory since the 1980s. Which three things converged around 2012 to make it practical?

Data, regulation and funding
Compute, robotics and translation

Computer vision
Reinforcement learning

q: What makes generative AI different from an ordinary classifier?

It works only on labelled images rather than on any text
It follows hand-coded rules instead of learning from data
It predicts continuous numbers instead of a category
why: Generative AI creates new text, images, audio or code rather than just classifying or predicting a label. LLMs like GPT are trained on massive text corpora to generate human-like language.

q: What is an LLM trained to do?
choices: Predict the next token given everything before it
Look up each answer in a database of verified facts
Classify every sentence as either positive or negative
Translate each token into one of a fixed set of labels
why: Training is next-token prediction on enormous corpora; grammar, facts and patterns emerge from scale. At use time it generates one token at a time by sampling from predicted probabilities.

q: What is the order of the deck's four simplified LLM steps?
choices: Tokenize → Predict next token → Learn from scale → Generate
Generate → Tokenize → Learn from scale → Predict next token
Learn from scale → Tokenize → Generate → Predict next token
Tokenize → Generate → Predict next token → Learn from scale
why: Text is broken into tokens (word pieces), the model is trained to predict the next token, it learns from huge corpora, and at use time it generates token by token.

q: Why can LLMs confidently state false information ('hallucination')?

Their training corpora deliberately contain no factual text at all
They are trained only on small datasets of a few hundred documents
They copy answers from a fact database that is out of date
why: The deck's caveat: LLMs predict plausible text and do not know facts the way a database does, so they can produce confident, fluent falsehoods.

q: 'Small, unexpected changes to the input cause surprisingly large errors' describes which limitation?

Hallucination
Data dependency
Lack of true understanding
why: That is brittleness. Hallucination is confident false statements, data dependency is inheriting the data's biases and gaps, and lack of understanding is pattern matching without comprehension.

q: Why did facial recognition historically show higher error rates for women and people with darker skin?

The cameras used could not capture those faces at all

choices: Regression: the output is a continuous number
Classification: the output is a category

q: In the course notation, what does m stand for?
choices: The number of training examples
The number of features
The slope of the hypothesis
The learning rate
why: m is the number of training examples (rows). Features are counted by n, the slope is θ₁, and the learning rate is α.

q: What does x⁽²⁾ mean in the course notation?
choices: The input of the 2nd training example
The input value squared
The 2nd feature of every example
The 2nd parameter, θ₂
why: The superscript in parentheses indexes the training example: (x⁽ⁱ⁾, y⁽ⁱ⁾) is the i-th example. It is not a power, and a feature is written with a subscript (x₂).

q: In h_θ(x) = θ₀ + θ₁x, written as y = b + wx, what are θ₀ and θ₁?
choices: θ₀ = b (intercept), θ₁ = w (slope)
θ₀ = w (slope), θ₁ = b (intercept)
θ₀ = x (input), θ₁ = y (target)
θ₀ = m (examples), θ₁ = α (rate)
why: θ₀ is the intercept/bias b and θ₁ is the slope/weight w. For the temperature data they are 32 and 1.8.

q: With θ₀ = 1 and θ₁ = 0.5, what is h_θ(x) at x = 3?
why: h = 1 + 0.5·3 = 2.5. 1.5 forgets θ₀; 3.5 and 4.5 come from adding the wrong terms.

q: Which parameter values give the flat line h(x) = 1.5?
why: A zero slope makes the line horizontal at the intercept. θ₀ = 0, θ₁ = 0.5 is the deck's line through the origin.

q: The learned temperature model is h(x) = 32 + 1.8x. What does it predict for 35 °C?
why: 32 + 1.8·35 = 32 + 63 = 95, which is the green point on the deck's plot. 113 °F is the answer for 45 °C, and 63 forgets the +32.

q: Which is the squared-error cost function used in 1.2?
choices: J(θ₀,θ₁) = (1/2m) Σ (h_θ(x⁽ⁱ⁾) − y⁽ⁱ⁾)²
J(θ₀,θ₁) = (1/m) Σ |h_θ(x⁽ⁱ⁾) − y⁽ⁱ⁾|
J(θ₀,θ₁) = (1/2m) Σ (h_θ(x⁽ⁱ⁾) − y⁽ⁱ⁾)
J(θ₀,θ₁) = (2/m) Σ (h_θ(x⁽ⁱ⁾) − y⁽ⁱ⁾)²
why: The 'squared error function' averages squared residuals with a 1/2m factor. The goal is to minimise it over θ₀ and θ₁.

q: Why does the cost function square the error and divide by 2m?
choices: Squaring stops + and − errors cancelling; the 2 cancels when differentiating
Squaring makes J negative near the minimum; the 2 halves the training set
Squaring speeds training up; the 2 counts the two parameters θ₀ and θ₁
Squaring keeps J below 1; the 2 doubles the effective learning rate
why: Squared errors are never negative, so they can't cancel. The ½ is a convenience: it cancels the 2 that comes down when you differentiate the square.

q: Points (1,1), (2,2), (3,3), with h = θ₁x (θ₀ = 0). What is J(0.5)?
why: Predictions 0.5, 1, 1.5 give squared errors 0.25 + 1 + 2.25 = 3.5, and 3.5/(2·3) ≈ 0.58. 1.17 forgets the 2 in 2m; 2.33 is J(0); 0 is J(1).

q: Points (1,2) and (2,4), with h = θ₁x and θ₁ = 1. What is J(θ₁)?
why: Errors are (1−2) and (2−4), so squares 1 + 4 = 5, and 5/(2·2) = 1.25. 2.5 divides by m only; 5 forgets the averaging.

q: Plotting J(θ₁) for the (1,1), (2,2), (3,3) data gives…
choices: A bowl-shaped parabola with its minimum at θ₁ = 1
A straight line that keeps falling as θ₁ grows
An S-shaped curve crossing 0.5 at θ₁ = 0
A parabola with its maximum at θ₁ = 1
why: J(1) = 0, J(0.5) = J(1.5) ≈ 0.58, J(0) = J(2) ≈ 2.33: a symmetric bowl whose bottom is the correct slope θ₁ = 1. With both θ₀ and θ₁ free it becomes a 3-D bowl.

q: In θⱼ := θⱼ − α·∂J/∂θⱼ, what is α?
choices: The learning rate
The derivative term
The number of examples
The regularization parameter
why: The slide labels α as the learning rate and ∂J/∂θⱼ as the derivative part. The update repeats until convergence, for j = 0 and j = 1.

q: At the current θ₁ the slope of J(θ₁) is positive. One gradient-descent step will…
choices: Decrease θ₁, moving it left toward the minimum
Increase θ₁, moving it right toward the minimum
Leave θ₁ unchanged until the slope reaches zero
Flip θ₁ to the negative of its current value
why: θ₁ − α·(positive) is smaller, so θ₁ moves left and downhill. With a negative slope you subtract a negative, so θ₁ increases.

q: If θ₁ already sits at a local minimum, a gradient-descent step…
choices: Leaves θ₁ unchanged, because the derivative is 0
Moves θ₁ exactly α units in the negative direction
Restarts θ₁ from zero to search for a better minimum
Doubles θ₁ because the slope changes its sign there
why: At a local optimum the slope is 0, so θ₁ := θ₁ − α·0 = θ₁.

q: What happens if the learning rate α is too large?
choices: It can overshoot the minimum, fail to converge or even diverge
It converges very slowly, taking many tiny steps to the minimum
It always lands exactly on the global minimum in one step
It stops after one iteration because the slope becomes zero
why: Too large overshoots and may diverge. Too small is the slow-but-steady case.

q: Do you need to decrease α over time for gradient descent to converge?
choices: No: the derivative shrinks near a minimum, so the steps shrink on their own
Yes: a fixed α always overshoots once it gets close to the minimum
Yes: α has to be halved every iteration or the algorithm diverges
No: once the cost starts falling, α is ignored by the update
why: Gradient descent can converge to a local minimum with α fixed, because the steps automatically get smaller as the slope flattens.

q: For h = θ₀ + θ₁x, what is ∂J/∂θ₁?
choices: (1/m) Σ (y⁽ⁱ⁾ − h_θ(x⁽ⁱ⁾))·θ₁
why: The θ₁ derivative carries the extra ·x⁽ⁱ⁾ factor. Without it you have ∂J/∂θ₀; the squared form is J itself.

q: When updating θ₀ and θ₁ in one iteration, you should…
choices: Compute both new values from the old θs, then assign both
Update θ₀ first, then use the new θ₀ when computing θ₁
Update only θ₁, because θ₀ stays fixed at its start value
Update θ₁ first, then recompute J before updating θ₀
why: Both parameters are updated together in each iteration, using the old values. Using the freshly updated θ₀ inside the θ₁ update is the classic mistake.

q: Data (1,2) and (2,4); start θ₀ = θ₁ = 0 with α = 0.1. After one gradient-descent step, what is θ₁?
why: h = 0, so the errors are −2 and −4. ∂J/∂θ₁ = (1/2)(−2·1 − 4·2) = −5, so θ₁ = 0 − 0.1·(−5) = 0.5. 1.0 forgets the 1/m, −0.5 flips the sign, and 0.3 is the new θ₀.

q: Same setup: data (1,2) and (2,4), θ₀ = θ₁ = 0, α = 0.1. After one step, what is θ₀?
why: ∂J/∂θ₀ = (1/2)(−2 − 4) = −3, so θ₀ = 0 − 0.1·(−3) = 0.3. 0.6 forgets the 1/m, and 0.5 is the new θ₁.

q: Running gradient descent on the temperature data from θ₀ = θ₁ = 0 converges to…
choices: θ₀ = 32, θ₁ = 0
why: It rediscovers F = 32 + 1.8·t from data alone: the intercept is 32 and the slope is 1.8.

q: On the bumpy J(θ₀, θ₁) surface (from Andrew Ng's course), two gradient-descent runs that start at nearby points…
choices: Can end up in different local minima
Always reach the same global minimum
Never move, because the surface is flat
Climb to the nearest peak instead
why: The figure shows two paths from neighbouring starts that descend into different valleys. Gradient descent finds a local minimum, which depends on where you start.

q: Which two approaches does 2.1 give for solving linear regression?
choices: Gradient descent and the normal equation
Gradient descent and the sigmoid function
The normal equation and one-vs-all
Polynomial features and regularization
why: Slide 3 sets up the lecture as gradient descent (iterative) vs the normal equation θ = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy (closed form).

q: With n features, the multivariable hypothesis is…
choices: h(x) = θ₀ + Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ θᵢxᵢ
h(x) = θ₀ · Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ θᵢxᵢ
h(x) = Σᵢ₌₁ᵐ θᵢ + xᵢ
h(x) = θ₀ + θ₁x + θ₁x²
why: Each feature gets its own weight; n is the number of features. For the deck's 3-feature data it is θ₀ + θ₁x₁ + θ₂x₂ + θ₃x₃. The last option is polynomial in a single x.

q: Why add a column x₀ = 1 to the data?
choices: So θ₀ becomes an ordinary weight and h(x) = Xθ works as one product
So that every feature is scaled to the same range before training
So the matrix XᵀX becomes the identity and needs no inversion
So the cost J(θ) can never become exactly zero during training
why: θ₀x₀ = θ₀ when x₀ = 1, so the intercept folds into the matrix product h(x) = Xθ.

q: A dataset has 5 examples and 3 features. After adding the x₀ column, what are the shapes of X and θ?
choices: X is 5×4, θ is 4×1
X is 5×3, θ is 3×1
X is 4×5, θ is 5×1
X is 5×4, θ is 5×1
why: One row per example and one column per feature plus the ones column gives 5×4. θ needs one entry per column (4×1), so Xθ is 5×1, one prediction per example.

q: θ = [32, 1.8, 0, 0] and one row of X is [1, 10, 12, 5]. What is the prediction h(x)?
why: 1·32 + 10·1.8 + 12·0 + 5·0 = 32 + 18 = 50, which matches y = 50 for that row. The normal-equation model predicts exactly 50 for this input.

q: θ = [1, 2, 0, 1] and x = [1, 3, 5, 2] (x₀ = 1 first). What is h(x) = xθ?
Temperature data y = [50, 59, 68, 77, 86], starting θ = 0 (so every prediction is 0). What is J(θ)?
why: The squared residuals sum to 2500 + 3481 + 4624 + 5929 + 7396 = 23930, and 23930/(2·5) = 2393. 4786 divides by m only; 340 is Σy.

q: What is the vectorised gradient-descent update for linear regression?
choices: θ := (XᵀX)⁻¹·Xᵀ·(h(x) − y)
why: Xᵀ(h − y) gives every partial sum Σ(h − y)·xⱼ in one product. You need Xᵀ, not X, for the shapes to match; the sign is minus to go downhill; and the last option mixes in the normal equation.

q: In the worked example Xᵀ(h − y) = [−340, −7250, −7635, −1845], with α = 0.001 and m = 5. What is θ₁ after one step from θ = 0?
why: θ₁ = 0 − 0.001·(1/5)·(−7250) = 1.45. 7.25 forgets the 1/m, −1.45 drops the minus sign, and 0.068 is θ₀.

q: Same step: the first entry of Xᵀ(h − y) is −340. What is θ₀ after the update, exactly?
why: 0.001·(1/5)·340 = 0.068. The slide prints 0.06 (truncated), but its next predictions such as 34.737 were computed with 0.068.

q: In the 2.1 example, what does the first entry of Xᵀ(h − y) equal?
choices: The plain sum of the residuals, because the x₀ row of Xᵀ is all ones
The sum of the squared residuals divided by twice the number of examples
The residual of the first training example multiplied by its x₁ value
The mean of the target vector y, because θ starts at zero
why: The first row of Xᵀ is [1,1,1,1,1], so that entry is Σ(h − y) = −340: the θ₀ gradient before the 1/m.

q: How did J change over the first three gradient-descent iterations in 2.1 (α = 0.001)?
why: After the first update the predictions jump from 0 to about 35–93, so J drops sharply to 62.625 and then to 61.25. It keeps falling (about 14 by iteration 900 in the code).

q: What is the normal equation?
choices: θ = (Xᵀ·X)⁻¹·(Xᵀ·y)
θ = (X·Xᵀ)⁻¹·(X·y)
θ = (Xᵀ·y)⁻¹·(Xᵀ·X)
θ = Xᵀ·(X·θ − y)
why: It solves for the optimal θ in one shot. The order matters: invert XᵀX, then multiply by Xᵀy.

q: For a design matrix X with a leading ones column and m = 5 rows, what is the top-left entry of XᵀX?
why: That entry is the dot product of the ones column with itself, Σ1 = m = 5. The slide's XᵀX starts with 5, and its next entry 100 is Σx₁.

q: In the 2.1 example, what is the first entry of Xᵀy?
choices: 340, the sum of all targets
50, the first target
68, the mean target
5, the number of examples
why: The ones row of Xᵀ times y adds up the targets: 50 + 59 + 68 + 77 + 86 = 340.

q: The normal equation returns θ = [32, 1.8, 2.8e−14, −1.7e−13]. How should you read the last two values?
choices: As floating-point noise: those features carry no information
As small but real weights that slightly improve predictions
As a sign the matrix inversion failed and θ is invalid
As the learning rate and number of iterations it used
why: Values around 10⁻¹⁴ are numerically zero. The model recovered F = 32 + 1.8·C exactly and correctly ignores x₂ and x₃.

q: Which is true of the normal equation compared with gradient descent?
choices: No learning rate and no iterations, but very slow with very many features
Needs a learning rate, but works best when there are very many features
Needs many iterations, but never has to invert any matrix at all
No learning rate, and it is fastest when there are very many features
why: Normal equation: no α, no iterations, must compute (XᵀX)⁻¹, slow when n is large. Gradient descent: choose α, many iterations, very good with many features.

q: You have a very large number of features. Which method does 2.1 recommend, and why?
choices: Gradient descent, because computing (XᵀX)⁻¹ becomes too slow
Normal equation, because it needs no learning rate to tune
Normal equation, because it finishes without any iterations
Gradient descent, because the normal equation needs a learning rate
why: No α and no iterations are real advantages of the normal equation, but inverting XᵀX gets very slow as n grows. That is where gradient descent wins.

q: In the 2.1 code, what does X_fin = np.hstack((np.ones((5,1)), X)) do?
choices: Adds the x₀ = 1 column, turning a 5×3 X into 5×4
Stacks y under X to form one 10×3 array
Normalises X so each column has mean 0
Transposes X from 5×3 into a 3×5 matrix
why: hstack places the ones column beside the 3 features, giving the (5, 4) design matrix printed on the slide.

q: In the training loop, which lines implement one gradient-descent step?
choices: delta = np.dot(X_fin.T, error); theta = theta − learning_rate*delta/m
delta = np.dot(X_fin, error); theta = theta + learning_rate*delta*m
delta = np.sum(error**2)/(2*m); theta = theta − learning_rate*delta
delta = np.linalg.inv(X_fin.T.dot(X_fin)); theta = delta.dot(error)
why: That is θ := θ − α·(1/m)·Xᵀ(h − y). The third option computes the loss, not the gradient; the fourth is the normal equation.

q: In the linear_regression notebook's normalization section, how is the test set standardised?
choices: With the training set's mean and standard deviation
With the test set's own mean and standard deviation
With the mean and std of the train and test sets combined

As z → +∞ and z → −∞, the sigmoid g(z) approaches…

0 and 1
+∞ and −∞

The model is wrong on 70% of the training examples

−log(h_θ(x)) − log(1 − h_θ(x))
y·log(h_θ(x)) + (1 − y)·log(1 − h_θ(x))

q: y = 1 and the model outputs h_θ(x) = 1. What is the cost?

q: Two examples: x⁽¹⁾ = [1, 0], y⁽¹⁾ = 1 and x⁽²⁾ = [1, 2], y⁽²⁾ = 0. Starting from θ = [0, 0] with α = 0.2, what is θ₁ after one step?

why: Slide 35: projecting (x₂ − x₁) on w/‖w‖ and using w·x = ±1 − b gives d = 2/‖w‖.

q: If w = (3, 4), what is the margin width 2/‖w‖?
Why is maximising 2/‖w‖ written as minimising ½‖w‖²?

Because the margin must be negative for minimisation
They are different problems; slide 36 is a mistake

To turn the dot product into a cross product
To guarantee w passes through the origin

choices: It gives one standard direction to project every point and compare distances
Because w must always be the largest support vector
Because the boundary passes through the origin

why: Slide 22: there are infinitely many points on the boundary to measure from, so we take the perpendicular as a reference and project all points on it.

choices: A scalar: |A||B|cos θ
A vector perpendicular to both
A unit vector along A
The angle θ between them

choices: It allows a few misclassifications, paying a penalty for each

why: Slide 40: the margin term plus C times the sum of hinge losses. The log term would be logistic loss.

q: Hinge loss for y = +1 and f(x) = 2?
why: 1 − 2 = −1, and max(0, −1) = 0. Outside the margin on the correct side costs nothing.

q: Hinge loss for y = −1 and f(x) = 0.5?
why: 1 − (−1)(0.5) = 1.5. The point is on the wrong side, so the loss is above 1.

why: Slide 42: for correctly classified points zeta = 0; for wrongly classified ones it is the distance from the correct margin line.

A hard-margin SVM
An error unless the data is linearly separable
